title: Kindness is the altar (Avot de-Rabbi Natan 4)
hook: at the ruined Temple, Yochanan ben Zakkai teaches: we have kindness, as it is written "I desire mercy" (Hosea 6:6)
tomorrow: what happens when Moses sits in on a class about Moses?

segments.voice: Yesterday, the fathers pleaded after the Temple fell, and only Rachel was answered, because she pleaded from mercy she had already shown. Rachel's plea. Same ruins today, and two sages standing in them.

When a place that mattered closes, the old diner, the summer camp, a grandparent's house, the ride home usually has two voices in it. One says: it's gone, and it's right to be wrecked about it. The other says: what made it matter is still here, in us. In a collection called Avot de-Rabbi Natan, two sages walk out of Jerusalem and have that exact argument, over a far larger loss. The Temple is in ruins.
screen: `A PLACE THAT MATTERED CLOSES.` → `TWO VOICES IN THE CAR.` → `THE TEMPLE IN RUINS.`

segments.voice: Rabbi Joshua looks at the rubble and says: woe to us. This was the place where Israel's wrongs were atoned for, and it's destroyed. His teacher, Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai, answers: my son, don't grieve. We have another atonement just as strong. Acts of loving-kindness, gemilut chasadim. And he quotes Hosea: "For I desire mercy, and not sacrifice." Now let each one make his case, because the tradition kept both. Rabbi Joshua: something holy really is gone. The altar was where a person could bring a wrong and set it down. Pretending that doesn't matter would be a lie, and Jewish life still mourns the Temple on Tisha b'Av. Rabban Yochanan: if atonement lived only in a building, it would have died with the building. But the prophet already said what God wants: mercy. So the altar moves, into kitchens and hospital rooms, a meal carried to a house of mourning. The Talmud even says loving-kindness is wider than charity: it can be done with your hands and your time, for rich and poor alike. One to tell a friend tonight: Pirkei Avot says the world stands on three things, and acts of loving-kindness is one of them. Neither sage loses this argument. Grief says the loss was real. Kindness says the work goes on.
screen: `WOE TO US: THE ALTAR IS GONE.` · `I DESIRE MERCY, NOT SACRIFICE.` · `THE GRIEF IS REAL.` · `THE ALTAR MOVES TO THE TABLE.` · then, large: `KINDNESS IS THE ALTAR.`

segments.voice: Choose one person who could use a small kindness today. Write them a text that gives instead of asks: a thank-you, an offer of help, a memory of them at their best. Send it now, or set it ready to send, and let it be today's offering.
Kindness is the altar: Rabban Yochanan's answer in the ruins. Acts of loving-kindness atone as the altar did, because God desires mercy.
Kindness is the new altar, and any table can hold one. Thirty-two in, eight to go.

howItsDone: Jewish life names gemilut chasadim, acts of loving-kindness, among the pillars of the world: visiting the sick, bringing meals to mourners, lending without interest, and attending weddings and funerals. The Temple is still mourned on Tisha b'Av.

chat.says: for sale sign went up in saba's yard. mom says don't be sad, it's just a house. is she right?
options: Both are true: the loss is real, and what the house held goes on in kindness.
She's right. Feeling sad about a house means you've missed the point.
No. Once the house is gone, everything it meant is gone with it.
chat.meaning: Rabbi Joshua grieved the ruins; Rabban Yochanan said kindness atones as the altar did. The tradition kept both the grief and the work.
